Furman enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 22-12 overall and 10-8 in Southern Conference play after winning the SoCon tournament as the No. 6 seed, beating Samford 86-81 on March 7, UNC Greensboro 81-75 on March 8, and ETSU 76-61 in the championship on March 9. Their regular-season profile was uneven, but the tournament run was real substance, not luck: they closed with three straight wins after ending the regular season with an 86-67 loss at Western Carolina on February 28. Furman’s path tells you exactly what this team is: dangerous when its shotmaking and ball movement sync up, vulnerable when opponents speed them up or turn the game into a physical rebounding-and-turnover fight. Furman’s official team averages through 34 games were 76.47 points per game on .476 shooting, .327 from three, and .690 at the foul line, while allowing 70.28 points per game on .413 opponent shooting. They averaged 38.0 rebounds and 15.6 assists per game. 

Offensively, Furman still looks like a Bob Richey team in structure: a read-heavy half-court attack built on spacing, inside-out play, and perimeter decision-making, but this year’s version leaned more on dribble penetration from Alex Wilkins and paint finishing from Cooper Bowser and Charles Johnston than some of Furman’s older, higher-volume three-point teams. Specific tendencies show up in game recaps. Against Richmond on November 27, Furman paired a one-three-one zone defensively with efficient half-court offense, hitting 6-of-11 first-half threes and building a 43-38 halftime lead before stretching the margin to 71-62 with 4:13 left; Asa Thomas hit his fifth three in that closing surge, showing Furman’s common action of driving, spraying, and then lifting shooters behind the play. Against Elon on December 3, Furman erased an 18-point deficit and scored 97, converting 18-of-20 free throws in the second half; that is a strong indicator that their offense is not just continuity motion for jumpers but also late-clock attack through downhill guards. In the SoCon title game on March 9, Furman shot 50.9% overall, went 10-for-26 from three, and grabbed 11 offensive rebounds, which is the clearest example of how dangerous they are when the shooting and second-chance game arrive together. 

The core named offensive pieces are clear. Alex Wilkins is the lead creator and primary perimeter scorer at 17.7 points and 4.7 assists per game over 34 games, shooting .458 from the field and .835 at the line. He is the late-clock bailout option and the player most likely to create a paint touch without a drawn set. Asa Thomas adds 12.4 points per game and shoots .389 from three, giving Furman a true spot-up and secondary-action scoring wing. Cooper Bowser is the interior efficiency piece at 14.0 points and 6.0 rebounds per game while shooting an elite .770 from the field; in the SoCon final he scored 21 points against ETSU. Charles Johnston averages 9.8 points and 9.1 rebounds and gives them a physical glass presence. Tom House adds 8.1 points and shoots .852 at the foul line, useful in late-game closing lineups. Furman’s offense is at its best when Wilkins collapses the defense, Bowser finishes around the rim, and Thomas or House punish help rotations.

Defensively, Furman is not a pure man-to-man pressure team. The specific documented tendency is change-of-pace zone, especially the one-three-one. Furman used a one-three-one zone to force 11 first-half turnovers against Richmond in a 73-72 win on November 27, and the same scheme has shown up in prior Bob Richey game-management patterns. This year’s numbers suggest the philosophy is to protect the arc enough to stay attached to shooters, finish possessions with rebounding, and selectively disrupt rhythm rather than gamble constantly: opponents shot .413 overall and .325 from three against Furman for the season. When Furman is locked in, the defense can look excellent. VMI shot just 26.9% against the Paladins in a 69-48 Furman win on January 10, and Furman held the Keydets to 6-for-25 inside the arc while winning the glass 48-32. Wofford was held without a field goal for 6:32 late in a 76-67 Furman road win on February 21, after trimming the margin to 60-59 with 7:42 left. Those are not abstract culture points; those are exact stretches that show Furman can tighten the screws when it identifies where the opponent is trying to score.

Bob Richey’s coaching philosophy is visible in those game scripts: tactical flexibility, controlled tempo, and willingness to change defenses midstream. The most documented in-game adjustment example is Richmond on November 27, when the one-three-one created 11 first-half turnovers and helped build separation. Another is Wofford on February 21, when Furman answered a 21-1 Terrier run spanning halftime by re-stabilizing the game, then held Wofford to two field goals over its final 15 attempts. A third is the March 8 SoCon semifinal against UNC Greensboro: Furman trailed badly in the first half, then rode a massive second-half shotmaking adjustment through Wilkins, who scored 34 points on 10-of-17 shooting, 4-of-7 from three, and 10-for-10 at the line to carry an 81-75 comeback win. That game is important for scouting because it shows Richey will flatten the decision tree late and let his best guard play with freedom rather than forcing equal-opportunity offense.

Clutch execution is one of Furman’s strongest tournament indicators. On December 31, Furman beat Mercer 74-72 when Wilkins drove right and hit an 8-foot jumper with 19 seconds left after Mercer had tied the game at 72 with 49 seconds remaining. On November 27, Furman beat Richmond 73-72 and held the Spiders to 1-of-7 shooting to close the game. On January 14, Furman won at Samford 77-73, a high-value road result later confirmed by the official box score, and on January 29 Furman beat Samford again, 78-73. On February 8, the loss to UNC Greensboro was instructive in the other direction: Furman cut the margin to one with 2:01 left, then turned it over, surrendered a Noah Norgaard three with 47 seconds left, and never fully recovered in a 67-64 defeat. That game revealed their late-game weakness: when Wilkins cannot create a clean advantage and the possession gets bogged down, the offense can turn static.

Recent form of the top players matters. Wilkins was outstanding down the stretch and especially in Asheville, averaging 21.7 points per game in the SoCon tournament and earning tournament MVP honors. His 34-point eruption against UNC Greensboro on March 8 matched Furman’s freshman single-game record. Bowser was equally important in the title run, averaging 16.3 points and 6.3 rebounds in the tournament, then posting 21 points in the 76-61 title win over ETSU. House averaged 12.0 points in the league tournament and hit 5-of-9 from three. Johnston’s season-long value is the rebounding base; he averaged 9.1 boards for the year and had a season-best 15 rebounds against VMI on January 10. Thomas remains the swing spacer: he averaged 12.4 points for the year and went 6-for-7 from three for 18 points in the February 21 win at Wofford.

The notable wins are revealing. Richmond on November 27, 73-72, showed Furman can beat a solid multi-bid-league opponent with defensive versatility and shotmaking. Elon on December 3, 97-88, showed comeback punch after trailing by 18. Furman’s January 23 road demolition of UNC Greensboro, 89-66, was their largest margin of victory in the series since 2006 and showed their ceiling when the offense gets downhill and the supporting shooters make teams pay. The March wins over Samford, UNCG, and ETSU are the most important because they came on consecutive days against top-half SoCon competition. The notable losses are just as informative. Western Carolina beat Furman 80-77 in overtime on January 3 and then 86-67 on February 28; that season split suggests Furman had trouble containing Western’s pace and pressure for full 40-minute stretches. ETSU beat Furman 75-71 in overtime on February 4, then Furman flipped that matchup 76-61 in the title game, which is the best adjustment example on the schedule. The February 8 home loss to UNCG, 67-64, exposed how Furman can be stalled by physical perimeter defense and late-clock possessions.

As for NCAA tournament history under Bob Richey, the Furman head coach previously reached the 2023 NCAA Tournament, where Furman won in the First Round by upsetting Virginia 68-67 before losing to San Diego State in the Second Round. The 2026 bid gives Richey his second NCAA tournament appearance as Furman head coach. That matters because he is not coaching his first one-game prep cycle anymore; he has already shown he can win a tournament game and can carry a mid-major team into March with a defined tactical identity.

Bottom line: Furman is not an upset pick because of romance or brand memory from 2023. They are an upset threat because they have a real primary creator in Wilkins, an elite-efficiency interior finisher in Bowser, a rebound anchor in Johnston, and a coach in Richey who has repeatedly shown documented willingness to toggle defenses, ride hot hands, and alter game texture from one matchup to the next.

([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-offensive-rating?utm_source=openai))

The offensive style data points in a familiar Furman direction, though not at vintage peak levels. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/stats-adv-efg-percent?utm_source=openai))

That creates a subtle but important divergence from conventional wisdom. The eye test for a program like Furman often says “dangerous shooting mid-major,” and the data only half-agrees. So this is not an offense overwhelming teams with elite three-point conversion or relentless paint attacks; rather, it is an offense that has been efficient overall because it avoids terrible shots and gets enough value from twos plus spacing to lift eFG%. In other words, the shot profile is stronger than the headline shooting percentage. That matters for upset equity: teams with high eFG% but only average 3PT% can be more stable than “hot shooting only” teams, but they also have less nuclear upside if they cannot manufacture free points at the stripe. matchup-analyst:
Furman enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a dangerous but very attackable offense-first team. Through the 2025-26 season, the Paladins were 22-12 after winning the SoCon tournament; before Asheville they were 16-10 in cumulative team stats, averaging 76.27 points per game, shooting 47.4% from the field, 32.0% from three, and only 67.0% at the line. Sports-Reference’s 2025-26 team page listed them at 76.8 points per game with a 112.7 offensive rating, 103.2 defensive rating, and 70.3 points allowed, which frames them as good enough offensively to beat quality teams but not so efficient that they can survive major disruption. Furman also averages 16.3 assists per game in the school cumulative stats, and WarrenNolan listed them at 15.7 assists per game nationally, which supports the eye test that this is primarily a ball-movement offense rather than an isolation-heavy one. ([furmanpaladins.com](https://furmanpaladins.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26?utm_source=openai))

Style-wise, Furman still wants to play through spacing, cutting, and frontcourt finishing rather than pure one-on-one shot creation. Cooper Bowser, a 6-foot-11 junior forward, is their best interior finisher at 13.7 points per game on 78.6% shooting, while 6-foot-7 senior Ben Vander Wal adds 8.2 points, 5.7 rebounds, and 2.5 assists on 69.0% shooting. That efficiency profile shows how much of Furman’s offense is built on assisted paint finishes, slips, interior seals, and drive-and-dump sequences instead of self-created pull-up volume. Furman’s disruption points are therefore clear: take away clean catches for Bowser, top-lock their shooters to kill reversal rhythm, and force late-clock creation from guards. Northern Iowa provided a clean example on November 14, 2025, holding Furman to 54 points, 4-of-30 from three, and just 14 assists on 22 field goals; Tom House went 0-of-7, Alex Wilkins 4-of-14, and Asa Thomas 0-of-4. That is the blueprint: flatten the movement game, stay attached to off-ball spacers, and make their secondary creators finish over length. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/furman/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Press and pressure do bother Furman when the game becomes turnover-driven. In the season opener against High Point on November 3, 2025, Furman lost 97-71 and committed 22 turnovers; High Point forced 11 in the first half alone, scored 25 points off those turnovers, and got 52 points in the paint. In the Troy game on November 7, 2025, Furman lost 64-61 while turning it over 13 times, and Troy finished with 17 steals and 9 fast-break points. Even in wins, pressure can distort Furman’s shot profile: Samford forced 14 turnovers on January 29, 2026, and outscored Furman 12-0 on points off turnovers despite losing 78-73. If you want to press them, the right version is not reckless full-court gambling; it is organized heat on the first pass and hard digs into the lane that force live-ball mistakes. Furman’s guards can pass against normal man-to-man, but they are less comfortable when entries are denied and the next action has to be improvised. ([furmanpaladins.com](https://furmanpaladins.com/news/2025/11/3/mens-basketball-furman-falls-to-high-point-in-field-of-68-tip-off-marathon-97-71.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Zone vulnerability is harder to prove directly from public play-type data, but the game evidence suggests compact coverage that clogs rhythm and dares their guards to make perimeter shots can work. The strongest example is still Northern Iowa: Furman scored 54, shot 13.3% from three, and got only 2 fast-break points. Because Bowser still produced 16 points on 7-of-10 shooting, UNI’s real win condition was not stopping the post entirely; it was shrinking the game around everyone else and forcing the Paladins’ jump shooters into low-efficiency volume. Illinois State also beat Furman 72-65 on November 28 while holding them to 25-of-55 shooting and just 6 free throws made. Furman can beat soft zone if the ball moves side-to-side, but a physical matchup zone or sagging man that looks like zone is effective because this roster does not have multiple elite downhill guards to bust it off the bounce. ([furmanpaladins.com](https://furmanpaladins.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/northern-iowa/boxscore/9511))

Preferred pace is moderate-to-fast by mid-major standards. Sports-Reference lists Furman at a 2025-26 pace of 68.9 possessions per game overall. Their worst nonconference loss, High Point, was played at 73.6 possessions; their ugly loss at Northern Iowa was slower at 64.7-ish game flow from the 54-70 final and official box score context, and Furman generated almost no easy offense. The lesson is matchup-dependent: Furman likes flowing possessions, but not chaotic ones they do not control. To force the opposite of their comfort, there are two viable plans. Against their depth and frontcourt skill, speed them up with ball pressure to create turnover basketball, as High Point did with 22 forced turnovers and 25 points off miscues. Or, if you have size and discipline, drag them into a half-court grind like Northern Iowa did, where every catch is contested and every weak-side cut is crowded. What does not work is playing at Furman’s preferred scripted tempo without disruptive coverage; in the SoCon title game against ETSU, Furman shot 50.9%, went 10-of-26 from three, won the glass 36-24, and looked very comfortable in a game it could execute. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/furman/men/2026-gamelogs-advanced.html?utm_source=openai))

Position-by-position, Furman has real size in the frontcourt but can be stressed athletically on the perimeter. At the 5/4, Bowser is 6-11 and Johnston is also 6-11; Vander Wal is 6-7 and Asa Thomas is a big 6-7 wing/guard. That gives them legitimate length at the 3/4/5 spots. However, the backcourt is more skill-oriented than explosive. Eddrin Bronson is 6-4, Alex Wilkins is a scoring guard, and Tom House is a movement shooter rather than a power driver. Against bigger power-conference guards, Furman’s 1 and 2 can be driven backward at the point of attack. Against truly mobile small-ball 4s, Furman’s bigger forwards can be pulled away from the rim. The reverse is also true: if your 4 is undersized, Bowser and Vander Wal can bury you on cuts, duck-ins, and second shots. The best way to attack their size is with speed at the guard spots and a stretch frontcourt that forces Bowser/Johnston into repeated perimeter decisions. The best way to survive their size is to front the post, bring late doubles from the baseline, and rotate off non-elite shooters. ([furmanpaladins.com](https://furmanpaladins.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster))

In isolation-versus-team-offense terms, Furman is much more team offense than isolation offense. The most concrete public indicator is the assist volume: 16.3 assists per game from Furman’s cumulative page and 15.7 from WarrenNolan. Using the cumulative team stats, that means assists account for roughly 58.8% of their made field goals (16.3 assists on 27.7 made field goals per game). That is a strong assisted-basket rate and supports the conclusion that Furman is at its best when actions connect into each other. When defenses force them off-script, the individual shot-making is more uneven. Northern Iowa is again the clean example: Furman made 22 field goals but only 14 assists, and the perimeter trio of House, Wilkins, and Thomas combined to shoot 4-of-25 from three and 4 turnovers. Conversely, in games where they are humming, the ball sticks less and multiple players feed the frontcourt. ([furmanpaladins.com](https://furmanpaladins.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26?utm_source=openai))

Transition offense is not their primary identity, but they will take it when turnovers create easy lanes. Against Troy they produced 9 fast-break points; against Northern Iowa they had only 2. Those two games matter because they show the range. If you let Furman run off steals or long rebounds, Wilkins and their wings can get downhill into early offense and Bowser runs to the rim hard. But if you convert your floor balance and force them to play against a set shell, the attack becomes much more ordinary. Transition defense is more concerning for Furman. High Point scored 52 points in the paint and punished their turnovers; Troy generated 9 fast-break points and 17 steals; Samford forced enough mistakes to create a 12-0 edge in points off turnovers even in defeat. Furman can be beaten before its half-court defense gets organized, especially after live-ball giveaways. ([furmanpaladins.com](https://furmanpaladins.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/troy/boxscore/9505))

Coaching adaptability under Bob Richey is real, and the SoCon tournament is the best recent evidence. Furman rallied from an 11-point halftime deficit to beat UNCG 81-75 in the semifinals on March 8, 2026, then won the title over ETSU 76-61 the next night as a No. 6 seed. That is not literally a playoff series, but it is the closest college analogue to multi-game adjustment pressure, and Furman showed it could change the game quickly. Furman also avenged earlier issues against Wofford by winning the rematch 76-67 on February 21 after withstanding a 21-1 Wofford run bridging halftime, then holding the Terriers without a basket for nearly seven minutes in the second half. So yes, the staff has shown in-season and tournament adjustment capacity. The caution is that adaptability has limits when athletic pressure overwhelms the guards, as seen in the High Point game and in the collapse at ETSU on February 4, when Furman blew a 15-point second-half lead and lost in overtime. ([furmanpaladins.com](https://furmanpaladins.com/news/2026/3/8/mens-basketball-furman-rallies-to-down-uncg-81-75-paladins-earn-fourth-socon-championship-appearance-in-five-years.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Concrete gameplan: To beat this team you must 1) pressure the first pass and make them initiate offense late; 2) crowd Bowser’s catches with a front-and-scram help plan rather than hard doubles every touch; 3) go under selectively on shaky pull-up threats but top-lock House and other movement shooters; 4) send athletic guards downhill at Furman’s backcourt to create paint collapse; 5) sprint back on every shot to erase their opportunistic transition; and 6) make them win with contested, late-clock jumpers. The exact target is simple: hold assists below their season norm, turn them over 14-plus times, and keep Bowser from getting efficient rim touches in rhythm. High Point showed the pressure blueprint with 22 Furman turnovers and 52 paint points. Northern Iowa showed the shell blueprint by holding Furman to 54 points, 4-of-30 from three, and only 2 fast-break points. If you combine those two models — pressure without losing floor balance — Furman becomes beatable.
